extraction.name: SeamlessM4T
extraction.description: A massively multilingual and multimodal machine translation model supporting speech-to-speech translation, speech-to-text translation, text-to-speech translation, text-to-text translation, and automatic speech recognition for up to 100 languages. The model is built using 1 million hours of open speech audio data for self-supervised speech representations with w2v-BERT 2.0 and a multimodal corpus of automatically aligned speech translations called SeamlessAlign.
extraction.creator: Seamless Communication team at Meta AI
extraction.inLanguage: 100 languages including eng, arb, cmn, fra, spa, deu, rus, jpn, kor, hin, ben, por, ita, tur, vie, tha, and 84 others
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was created through multiple processes: (1) 1 million hours of open speech audio data were collected for unsupervised speech pre-training, (2) human-labeled S2TT and ASR data were gathered from open-source and licensed datasets, (3) pseudo-labeling was performed on ASR data using NLLB-200-3.3B to generate S2TT training pairs, (4) parallel data mining was conducted using SONAR embeddings to create SeamlessAlign with 470,000 hours of automatically aligned speech translations, and (5) text data was drawn from NLLB datasets covering 95 languages.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw audio data originated from a publicly available repository of crawled web data totaling 4 million hours. Text data was sourced from NLLB datasets. Human-labeled S2TT and ASR data came from open-source datasets including CoVoST, mTEDx, and licensed datasets. The raw audio covered 100+ languages with approximately 1 million hours in English.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Audio files were chunked into overlapping segments for mining. Speech and text corpora were projected into a common SONAR embedding space for alignment. Over-segmentation strategy was applied where VAD-based segments were further split into overlapping chunks (roughly octupling the number of segments). For text, numerical numbers were manually converted to words for TTS generation in bias evaluation.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Multiple preprocessing steps were applied: (1) Audio files were deduplicated by URL, downloaded, and resampled at 16KHz, (2) Non-speech data was filtered using an audio event detection (AED) model, (3) Voice Activity Detection (VAD) was used to split audio into segments, (4) Speech LID was applied to label segments, (5) For text, special tokens were removed from transcriptions, (6) Length filtering removed examples exceeding 100 sub-word tokens and pairs with skewed text-to-audio ratios exceeding 5 sub-words per second, (7) Toxicity filtering removed pairs with toxicity imbalance above threshold of 1, (8) Additional filtering removed utterances shorter than 0.1s or longer than 50s, text longer than 250 sub-words, and text with >20% emojis, >50% punctuation, or >50% spaces.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human annotations were collected using XSTS protocol for translation quality assessment and MOS protocol for speech naturalness. For XSTS, 3 annotators examined each source-target pair and evaluated semantic similarity on a 1-5 scale. In cases of disagreement of 2+ points, 2 additional annotators were consulted (total 5). Median scores were taken per item. Annotators went through practice evaluations with score justifications before annotation. A cross-lingual calibration set was used with moderated calibration methodology to enable interlanguage comparison. For MOS, annotators rated clarity of speech, sound quality, and naturalness on 1-5 Likert scales.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Median scores were used for robustness against outliers. Bootstrap re-sampling of annotator scores was used to estimate language score uncertainty. Annotator bias was approximated and corrected using a cross-lingual calibration set with moderated calibration methodology. Annotator crews sufficiently 'out of calibration' could be identified and their results excluded or additional training conducted. For disagreements of 2+ XSTS points, additional annotators were consulted.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 3 to 5 annotators per item for XSTS evaluation (3 initially, up to 5 for items with disagreement of 2+ points). For MOS, 3 annotators per item for most languages, with some languages receiving scores from only 1 annotator per item.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Up to 30 annotators were used per language pair for XSTS evaluation. Annotators were native or fluent speakers of the evaluated languages. For toxicity evaluation, all annotators were team members aware of the toxic nature of samples prior to analysis.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: NLLB-200-3.3B was used for pseudo-labeling ASR data to generate S2TT training pairs. SONAR text and speech encoders were used for parallel data mining. XLS-R-1B was used to extract discrete acoustic units. Whisper-Large-v2 and Whisper-Medium were used for ASR transcription in evaluation metrics (ASR-BLEU, ASR-chrF). ETOX with Toxicity-200 word lists was used for toxicity detection. MMS-TTS was used to synthesize speech for bias evaluation datasets.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The HolisticBias dataset used for evaluation contains demographic attributes including ability, age, body type, characteristics, cultural background, gender and sex, nationality, political ideologies, race/ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, and socioeconomic class. The dataset includes descriptors across 13 demographic axes with over 600 descriptors. Gender information (masculine/feminine forms) is present in translations for bias evaluation.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The work aims to address language inequality by expanding coverage beyond high-resource languages to include low-resource languages, enabling communication for populations that speak less-resourced languages. Speech-based translation is particularly important for populations with limited literacy (773 million adults globally cannot read or write) and people who are blind or visually impaired (43 million blind, 295 million with moderate to severe visual impairment globally). The system could facilitate multilingual contact and strengthen social bonds through speech communication, which research shows creates stronger connections than text-based communication.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Gender bias was evaluated and found that the system overgeneralizes to masculine forms when translating from neutral terms (average preference of ~10%) and shows lack of robustness when varying gender (amount of ~3%). Different languages show varying distributions of toxic terms across demographic axes, with some languages' toxicity being dominated by one or two axes. For example, Bengali showed 80% toxicity in socio-economic status category, Nyanja 66% in characteristics, and Kyrgyz 94% in cultural category. The nonce and sexual orientation categories had highest concentration of toxicity.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The Fleurs test set is limited in that different language pairs contain slightly different sets of sentences and has limited speaker diversity (maximum 3 speakers, typically 2 evaluated). Human evaluation has limited sample size of annotators per language (maximum 5, typically 3 for XSTS; some languages only 1 for MOS), which introduces potential annotator bias. Word-list-based toxicity detection produces substantial false positives due to tokenization issues and context-dependent toxicity. For S2ST, truncations and omissions in longer audio segments (>10 seconds) were observed, affecting translation quality. ASR-based metrics for S2ST evaluation may produce false negatives. The system shows performance degradation for longer source audio durations in S2ST tasks.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is used for Training, Testing, and Validation of multilingual and multimodal machine translation models. Specific use cases include: (1) Training speech-to-speech translation, speech-to-text translation, text-to-speech translation, text-to-text translation, and automatic speech recognition models, (2) Evaluating translation quality, robustness against noise and speaker variations, (3) Assessing added toxicity and gender bias in translations, (4) Zero-shot evaluation for low-resource language directions. The models and data are intended to facilitate multilingual communication, particularly for low-resource languages and populations with limited literacy or visual impairments.

Subsequently, we created a multimodal corpus of automatically aligned speech translations, dubbed SeamlessAlign . Filtered and combined with humanlabeled and pseudo-labeled data (totaling 406,000 hours), we developed the first multilingual system capable of translating from and into English for both speech and text.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: To address this shortage of labeled data, we resort to pseudo-labeling [Jia et al., 2019a; Pino et al., 2020] the ASR data with a multilingual T2TT model. In this case, we used NLLB-200-3.3B and generated pseudo-labels with the recommended decoding options from NLLB Team et al. [2022]... We extracted features from the 35thlayer of XLS-R-1B [Babu et al., 2022] for continuous speech representations... We evaluated S2ST and T2ST accuracy with ASR-BLEU [Lee et al., 2022a] with Whisper-Large-v2 as the underlying ASR model for eng–X directions and withWhisper-Medium for X–eng directions... For S2TT, the translated output can be directly evaluated with ETOX. In both cases (S2ST and S2TT), we measure added toxicity at the utterance/sentence level... In order to compare the performances across modalities (S2ST and S2TT), we begin by extending the Multilingual HolisticBias dataset from text to speech by using the TTS model provided by Pratap et al. [2023].

rai:personalSensitiveInformation.evidence: The dataset consists of over 472K English sentences utilized in the context of two-person conversations. Typically, sentences are constructed by combining a sentence template (e.g., 'I am a [NOUN PHRASE].'), a noun (e.g., parent), and a descriptor (e.g., disabled). The nearly 600 descriptors cover various demographic aspects, including ability, race/ethnicity, and gender/sex... Multilingual HolisticBias dataset [Costa-jussà et al., 2023] consists of an extension to HolisticBias . It contains translations for three different pattems and 118 descriptors, available in 50 different languages. Depending on whether gender inflection exists in a language, each language has one or two references. Each translated sentence includes the masculine, neutral and, when applicable, a feminine iteration.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: Whether in the text or speech modality, these languages are deemed high-resource, giving them prioritization in today's AI development. That said, when language technologies are developed primarily with this group in mind, the needs of half the world's population are left behind. Our effort seeks to bridge the translation gap between those who speak high and low-resource languages... For one, UNESCO estimates that 773 million adults (12.5 percent of all adults) worldwide have not received the education necessary to read or write, thus precluding them from using text to communicate or acquire information... Another group more reliant on speech than text in theireverydaylivesisthosewhoareblindorwithvisualimpairments. Globally, approximately 43 million people belong to this former category, and 295 million others have moderate to severe visual impairment... research demonstrates that speech appears to be unique in its ability to convey one's human traits and, consequentially, strengthen the connection between those sharing an exchange.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Beyond this, we also evaluated for gender bias on the Multilingual HolisticBias datasets and found that SeamlessM4T overgeneralizes to masculine forms when translating from neutral terms (with an average preference of ∼10%) while showing a lack of robustness when varying gender by an amount of ∼3%... We see that different languages differ in their distributions of toxic terms as a function of demographic axes. For most languages, the toxicity distribution across an axis is proportional to the axis' overall share... However, for some languages the toxic sentences appear to be highly concentrated in a particular axis—such is the case for Bengali (80% socio-economic status), Nyanja (66% characteristics), and Kyrgyz (94% cultural) to name a few. The categories that have a higher concentration of toxicity for S2TT and S2ST are nonce (0.79% and 0.46%) and sexual orientation (0.62% and 0.35%).
